Analysis by Richard Cowan 

The Iraq and Afghan wars have greatly increased our awareness of how serious and prevalent the problem of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) can be. For a long time it was thought that PTSD was only associated with the most extreme violence of war, (shellshock), but we have learned the hard way that it is much more common a consequence of other sources of violence. 

The National Institute of Mental Health says, “Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, PTSD, is an anxiety disorder that can develop after exposure to a terrifying event or ordeal in which grave physical harm occurred or was threatened. Traumatic events that may trigger PTSD include violent personal assaults, natural or human-caused disasters, accidents, or military combat.” 

Just as some people have greater problems with physical wounds, the invisible wounds of war are not the same for everyone. Over the years that I have been involved in fighting cannabis prohibition, I have met many of its victims. Very few of them had actually suffered serious physical trauma directly inflicted by the police, althuogh medical patients had often endured what amounted to torture when they were deprived of their medicine. 

However, what both they and their families had suffered perfectly matched the NIMH’s description of the causes of PTSD: “a terrifying event or ordeal in which grave physical harm occurred or was threatened.” 

One or more family members were “taken hostage” (arrested); a huge “ransom” (bail) was extorted; and they were publicly humiliated, and often had the rest of their families threatened with further retaliation. (There is no need for a parenthetical definition these events, because that is exactly what happens.) 

Although the NIMH says that both natural or human-caused disasters can cause PTSD, I have noticed one major difference between the reactions to natural and human-caused disasters. After a terrible storm in which someone has been killed, the surviving family and friends are less likely to ask “Why”, than is the case when people have been killed by human action, like one of the recent campus shootings. 

Victims of the Drug War are often incredulous that the police and prosecutors could be so needlessly cruel. 

For example, how could someone arrest a quadriplegic for a few grams of cannabis?

See 

Georgia Quadriplegic Sentenced To 7-Year Prison Sentence Now Faces Up To 10 More Years In Prison After Indictment For Possession Of 36 Grams Of Marijuana.

There have now been almost 20 million marijuana arrests in the US alone, and most of these people have family and friends who are also victims. Sometimes they lose custody of their children, so the trauma continues into future generations. 

See 

How the War On Marijuana To Save The Children Has Become A War On the Children To Save Marijuana Prohibition 

The point is that the violence of the Drug War, especially the war on cannabis users, has a much wider and longer lasting impact on the lives of all the victims than can be seen on the related paper work. In fact, I think that it is very shortsighted to think that the whole of society is not traumatized by this violence which permeates our society, and not just as it impacts the direct victims as I have described. 

See 

The Theory and Practice of Chaos – Analysis By Richard Cowan 

The Paradox of State Terrorism As Deterrent. 

For every person arrested, and their family and friends, the trauma has to be felt through out society for there to be any “deterrent effect” in the laws. That is why there used to be brutal public executions. The police and prosecutors are only satisfied by the very deliberate acts that traumatize society… or would if they did not deny that they happen. 

I have written frequently about the fact that the media will not report the number of marijuana arrests, or the consequences of being arrested, much less being prosecuted and imprisoned. 

See 

Arresting Developments: 2003 Cannabis Arrests Hit All-Time High In DEAland, Decline In UK and Canada. Deaths Related to One Drug Soar In Holland. Guess Which One. 

and 

Lies Have Consequences. From Prohibitionist Venom to the Harsh Realities of Life and Death for Patients. Swedish Prohibitionists, Canadian Bureaucracy and DEAland Medical Murder. 

I call this phenomenon “stealth terrorism” because it does all of the things that state terrorism does, but it loses the deterrent effect, because they deny that it is happening. Now think that leaves the victims. 

1. They are surprised by what has happened to them. Why me? 

2. An amazing number of Americans still think that the Constitution protects them. They feel betrayed. 

3. They spend time in jail where they are stripped of their dignity, and surrounded by a violent bedlam. 

4. Their neighbors think that they must have been doing something more than “just having marijuana.” After all, no one is arrested just for that! So they are even more isolated. 

5. Either their families are ruined by staying with them, or they lose their families.

6. If they are medical users, their condition worsens and their doctors give them more and more potent pharmaceuticals until they have difficulty functioning.

7. Their lawyer is either convinced that they are “druggies” and deserve what happens to them, or is simply to overworked to be able to do a decent job defending them for what little they can pay. 

8. They lose their jobs and have take a menial job and are forced to urinate on demand, and are otherwise regularly degraded. 

9. They are forced to express remorse before an alcoholic judge for having used cannabis. 

10.At some point they are allowed to return to society, and are expected to feel grateful, even though their record keeps them from going to college or getting into many professions. 

Multiply that by 20 million, plus families and friends, and we have a society with a huge but hidden number of people with PTSD. (And this would not be a good time to suggest that cannabis might help them cope.) 

See 

Prophylactic State Violence: The Arrogance and Ignorance of Psychiatric Quackery. Bad Science, Worse Ethics -- Analysis by Richard Cowan 

If there is any single phrase that captures our state of denial, it is the classic from so many crime scenes: “Move along! There is nothing here for you to see.” 

That is generally good advice, but not when the crime has been committed in YOUR name. If we turn our backs on the victims we become complicit in the crimes and become prisoners of our own cowardice. There are worse things that can happen to our bodies, but there is nothing worse for the soul.
